cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf population and selections from it
processing: Traditional gongfu black tea method, with oxidation kept on the tender side to favour freshness and low bitterness.
harvest_season: Mostly spring tea, with a smaller share of autumn tea.
appearance_dry: Plump, tight, dark glossy strands with sharp tips and visible golden down.
appearance_liquor: Bright, vivid red, with a golden ring at the rim of the cup.
appearance_wet: Plump, tender and bud-rich, an even bright red.
taste_profile: Sweet aroma with a chestnut-and-caramel note, fresh and full in the mouth, low in bitterness, with a long sweet aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Large-leaf black tea gives a lot quickly, so pour off fast in the first steeps. Porcelain keeps the sweet aroma clear.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, mostly as spring tea, with some cheaper autumn lots. Like most Dian Hong it is meant for drinking fresh, within a year or two, rather than for ageing. Look for the geographical indication mark on protected products.
description:
Changning black tea comes from Changning county in Baoshan, on Yunnan's western tea belt next to Fengqing. It counts as an important part of Dian Hong and has its own protected name.

The tea uses Yunnan large-leaf plants and selections from them, picked mostly in spring. Makers keep to the traditional gongfu method and oxidise on the tender side, aiming for freshness rather than weight.

The result is a vivid red cup, often with a golden ring, smelling of sweetness and chestnut caramel. It is full but not very bitter, and the sweetness lasts. Steep it briefly; a long first steep hides what makes it nice.

The protected area covers ten townships of the county, including Tianyuan, Mangshui and Wenquan. Ask for the harvest season, because spring and autumn lots differ in price and depth.
history:
Black tea came late to this old tea county. After the Shunning experimental factory began Dian Hong in 1938, growers in bordering Changning tried making it too, without a real breakthrough.

That changed in 1955, when state tea companies sent staff to arrange a shift from green to black tea and brought technicians in to train workers. Twenty-one primary processing units were built within a year. In 1958 the new county factory made 2,463 dan of refined black tea and exported its first 123 tonnes.

The name gained a certification trademark in 2013, and geographical indication protection followed on 19 June 2015.
